newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - New brewers set to make Egypt market bubble.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New brewers set to make Egypt market bubble.

text.p: Egyptian drinkers can look forward to a good head on their beer before the end of the century when private companies will add sparkle to a market flattened by years under the government's thumb.
It took privatisation of the country's monopoly brewery, al-Ahram Beverages Company (ABC), earlier this year to get giant international firms sniffing out the Egyptian market.

Danish firm Carlsberg, cheered by ABC's new management, has signed a deal with the firm to build and operate a $50 million brewery, which will begin producing Carlsberg's "Green Label" beer in Egypt by 1999.
Local business tycoon Samih Sawiris of Orascom has also teamed up with Germany's Loewenbraeu to set up a $30 million brewery in el-Gouna, a Red Sea hamlet he has developed into a high-profile resort.
Another businessman, Farid Wadie Saad of the Egyptian Finance Company, said earlier this year he would set up yet another brewery before the beginning of 1998.
Beer fans who have been swilling the local Stella or paying astronomical prices for imports, are beaming.
BAD QUALITY LOCAL BEER MEANS MORE BUSINESS
Ahmed el-Zayat, the new executive chairman of ABC, says that one of his main tasks was defining what a Stella tasted like and Danbrew, a unit of Carlsberg, was hired to do just that.
"The workers would bottle any batch that was brewed, regardless of what it tasted like or what went into it. They got paid by the batch, you see," Zayat told Reuters.

Stella's inconsistent taste has evolved into an Egyptian legend. Tourists can buy t-shirts reading "If Stella doesn't kill you, it will make you stronger," while local drinkers often swap stories about the cockroaches and unidentified floating objects they find in their beer.
Hotels and restaurants, tired of customer complaints about flat Stellas, have recently begun offering imported beers but crippling duties and taxes have put a damper on their business.
The opportunities, Sawiris says, are brimming.

"We all know that Stella is a health hazard," he told Reuters. "We're initially targeting the import market because it's ridiculous to spend millions of dollars a year buying beer when we can do it locally."

"After that we'll break into the mainstream local market, which has been dominated by ABC and our edge is that we'll be able to produce our first brew by March 1998, definitely before they can revamp the factory and before Carlsberg," he added.
MORE BRANDS TO HIT MARKET SOON

Market statistics estimate alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer consumption in Egypt at around 530,000 hectolitres a year. For years, ABC has supplied 90 percent of alcoholic and 95 percent of non-alcoholic malt beverages. Imports make up the rest.

Sawiris expects the market to grow a little each year as the number of tourists visiting Egypt rises but a government ban on advertising alcoholic beverages and a new and improving ABC will prove tough competition.

Zayat, nicknamed "Rabso" by his employees after a local detergent brand, is determined to whip ABC back into shape, introduce new brands and wash out what he calls the "unimaginable corruption" riddling the firm.
"We are until now a market monopoly but we're not acting like one," said Zayat, a member of the U.S.-based Luxor Group, which bought out the government's share in ABC for $68 million.

"The company was run like a mafia. It was badly managed, the employees would drink the beer on the bottling line, managers would cut production to create a demand in the market, then sell the product at a premium that went in their pockets," he added.
According to Zayat, ABC will not only repackage and re-brew Stella, but it will also start producing Stella Premium, a darker, more alcohol-rich brew.
Non-alcoholic Stella, the only brand that will be heavily promoted, will be on the shelves by August. Zayat hopes some of that publicity will also spill over on to his alcoholic beers.
ISLAM CURBS BEER DRINKING, OR DOES IT?

Although stock brokers said that religious opposition was one of the main reasons the government only sold 25 percent of ABC through a 1996 share offering, both Zayat and Sawiris play down its effect on the market.
Drinking alcohol is forbidden by Islam, the main religion in Egypt, but it is legal in Egypt and many people do it anyway.

According to Zayat, the majority of Stella drinkers come from the lower classes and the southern provinces, the same demographic sources of the militants fighting to transform Egypt into a strict Moslem state.
"A bottle of beer is cheaper than a pack of cigarettes. Some people in Egypt just don't think drinking beer is a sin because of the relatively low alcohol content," Zayat said.
International securities house HSBC James Capel says beer consumption in Egypt is very low compared to other Moslem countries like Malaysia and Turkey.
Apart from a booming tourist industry, ABC and Sawiris are banking on Egypt's status-conscious and mainly youthful population and their ever increasing purchasing power to keep them in the black.
MARKET DESTINED TO BE TINY BY GLOBAL STANDARDS

Rosy outlooks aside, analysts say that Egypt's beer market is destined to remain small by international standards, especially compared to North African states like Morocco and Tunisia, where drinking alcohol is more socially permissible.
Armed with an aggressive marketing strategy, Sawiris and Zayat are determined not to let religion get in their way.
"The market in Egypt will never get as large as other North African states because of how religious people are here, but, then again, there's definitely potential for growth.
"We wouldn't be doing this if we didn't think it worthwhile. Business is business," Sawiris said.
